name: Liam Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have a bachelor’s degree and lead four motor-claims clerks at an insurer. I earn more than the typical clerk because I can reconcile repair photographs with workshop bills; I use AI now and then to summarise emails, never to settle a claim. My partner Bea works at a library, we have no children and we pay a mortgage together. We have saved eight months of expenses and there are plenty of other insurers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the motor claims desk that a little faster filing is useful, but a repair estimate still needs a person to ask what actually broke. I sometimes use AI to summarise workshop emails and then check each line against the photographs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead four clerks and earn a higher wage because I can untangle three workshops billing for one collision. My partner Bea works in a library, we have no children and our eight-month reserve makes the mortgage manageable while both wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my Tuesday check of disputed repair invoices and put 180 a month into the house reserve while both wages hold. In the first year I would use the email summary only after comparing it with the workshop photograph and signed estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our jobs and mortgage now. A neat workshop email does not show which wheel was bent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill needed a closer look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A garage billed for two doors after a sideswipe that damaged one. I called the workshop and got the second door removed before payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you teach that check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the junior clerk the photograph and the line on the estimate. I would not ask them to trust my memory of the call.

say: I would keep **repair photographs** beside workshop estimates before approving each motor claim.
I would use **AI summaries occasionally**, then verify them against photos and signed estimates.
think: I have **eight months saved** with Bea’s present library wage.
I know **invoice detail** protects claimants and the insurer.
do: **Check disputed invoices** every Tuesday against workshop photographs and signed estimates.
**Save 180 monthly** while both current wages cover the mortgage and basic bills.
S0.quote: A neat workshop email does not show which wheel was bent.
fieldNote: His **motor-claims skill** lies in matching workshop repair lines to photographs of actual vehicle damage.
The **eight-month reserve** was built on current household wages and does not prove future security.

steps.text: Check disputed motor repair invoices every Tuesday against photographs
Save 180 monthly while both household wages cover mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say Steady Disruption may write claim replies and compare repair estimates before clerks open a file. I would ask our workplace group for paid time to check rejected repairs and see the error log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own lead hours could be reduced if one person watches more automated files, even though I have eight months saved. Bea’s library wage would help, but it would not cover our full mortgage and bills alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a two-hour paid pilot next month to learn the new AI damage-checker on invented motor claims, with our normal hours protected. If approved I would learn the checker and bring missed damage lines to the workplace group; if my own hours fall, I would check actual nearby motor-claims posts and net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my hours, but I want a fair test. I do not want a fast estimate to hide a repair the driver still needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your workplace group ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The group would ask how many paid review hours remain and who signs a rejected repair. We can request that in writing; we cannot assume the manager agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a job suitable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take a new title just because it sounds technical. The posted net pay would have to cover our share of the mortgage, food and travel.

say: I would seek **paid checking hours** and an error log for the new damage-checker.
I would learn the **new AI damage-checker** on invented claims with protected current hours.
think: I could lose **lead hours** when automated files multiply.
I cannot fund our **full mortgage** from Bea’s wage alone.
do: **Learn the AI damage-checker** if approved for a paid pilot with normal hours protected in writing.
**Take missed damage lines** to the workplace group if approved.
**Check posted local jobs** if hours fall and net pay covers essentials.
S1.quote: I do not want a fast estimate to hide a repair the driver still needs.
fieldNote: His **two-hour pilot needs approval** and protected paid hours before he can run it next month.
The **workplace group request** cannot guarantee staffing levels or a paid local opening elsewhere.

steps.text: Learn new AI damage-checker if approved for paid pilot with current hours protected
Bring pilot errors to workplace group for paid review hours if approved
Check posted local motor-claims jobs if hours fall and net pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our team AGI by 2028 could compare estimates, draft letters and answer drivers more cheaply than clerks. Robots doing hands-on vehicle inspection may come around 2031, after our desk work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead claims post could vanish, but I do not know the firm’s staffing plan. Eight months saved gives Bea and me time to search; her library pay alone does not meet the mortgage and all our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written cut notice now and keep the reserve for the mortgage instead of buying a repair course on a guess. If my job ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply to actual paid local vehicle inspection openings only if I meet their safety requirements and net pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing my own wage, though I can see a plan while the reserve lasts. I cannot pay a mortgage with a job title that has no hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you qualified to inspect vehicles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have looked at inspection work, but I do not hold the safety credential needed for most posts. I would only enrol if an employer offers paid training with protected hours, not assume a quick course makes me qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would physical work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around 2031, robots could take vehicle inspections too. I would treat a paid inspection job as a bridge if offered, not a permanent shelter.

say: I would explain **claims desk work** faces AGI by 2028.
I would mention **inspection robots** may follow around 2031.
think: I think my **lead post could vanish**, without a cut notice.
I know **Bea’s wage alone** cannot cover our full budget.
do: **Request written cut notice** and protect mortgage reserve now.
Apply to **paid inspection posts** after loss only with safety credentials and bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss, with eight months to search.
S2.quote: I cannot pay a mortgage with a job title that has no hours.
fieldNote: An **inspection bridge** is conditional on a safety credential, real local openings and sufficient net pay for the mortgage.
He recognises **robots around 2031** could later shrink hands-on vehicle work, even if an inspection job appears.

steps.text: Request written claims cut notice and preserve eight-month mortgage reserve
Apply to qualified paid inspection posts after 2028 loss if net pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 gives us time to press for paid checks on motor claim decisions and train for other work. Robots capable of physical inspections may follow about 2034, so a field job may buy time rather than last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn more about vehicle inspection while still earning my lead wage, but I need the safety credential and supervised hours. I would not use our mortgage reserve for an unfunded course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a nearby inspection firm for its written safety requirements and an actual paid supervised opening, and ask my insurer about protected paid training time. Only if both exist would I enrol and practise; after 2031 job loss I would apply to a qualified post only where net pay covers our full budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possible end of my desk role, but five years gives me room to check the route. A training leaflet is not a paid inspection shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has to be in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need written training costs, paid hours and who signs off the safety work. If either employer cannot name those, I would stay on the claims rota and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does inspection work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even a real inspection post might shrink around 2034. I would ask how long the paid contract lasts before taking it.

say: I would seek **paid supervised inspection** with safety training.
I would treat **2034 robots** as a later risk to physical work.
think: I need **safety credentials** and actual paid supervised shifts before changing from claims to inspections.
I cannot spend **mortgage reserves** on an unverified course while my current wages still pay the bills.
do: **Check written safety requirements** and actual paid supervised openings now.
**Request protected training time** and enrol only if both employers agree.
**Apply after 2031 loss** only if qualified net wages cover our budget.
feel: **Anxious** about later desk-job loss, with time to verify a route.
S3.quote: A training leaflet is not a paid inspection shift.
fieldNote: The **training route** requires an actual paid opening, safety rules and protected current hours.
Inspection is a **temporary bridge** because hands-on robots follow around 2034.

steps.text: Check local inspection safety rules and actual paid supervised openings
Request protected paid training and enrol only if both employers agree
Apply after 2031 loss to qualified paid post if net wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us about ten years to protect claims appeal rights and build savings. Inspection robots may follow around 2039, after the desk work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage and present wages feel secure for the next few years, though I am only 27 and need many more earning years. I could pay down the loan steadily while checking real job routes each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking disputed motor invoices, pay an extra 120 toward the mortgage each month while both wages hold and ask the workplace group for annual paid-review staffing figures. If my role ends after 2036, I would pursue only posted local work I am qualified for with net wages covering our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the long end of the decade but steady about our bills now. A lower loan balance would give us more choices if the desk shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What staffing figure matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many hours are paid for an appeal review, not just how many files the system closes. That tells us whether people can still challenge a wrong repair decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep paying extra if wages fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would not use Bea’s future wages as a guarantee. Extra mortgage payments stop if either current income falls.

say: I would ask for **paid appeal hours** before 2036.
I would keep **repair decisions reviewable** by a person.
think: I feel **secure near term** with present wages and savings.
I need **later paid work** if claims shrink.
do: **Check motor invoices** while present role pays.
**Pay 120 extra monthly** toward mortgage while both wages hold.
**Ask group annually** for paid review hours; check qualified paid openings after loss.
S4.quote: A lower loan balance would give us more choices if the desk shrinks.
fieldNote: His **mortgage prepayment** depends on two current wages and stops if either falls.
His **future work** depends on a real qualified vacancy and net pay covering bills.

steps.text: Check disputed motor invoices every Tuesday while role pays
Pay 120 extra toward mortgage monthly while both present wages hold
Ask workplace group annually for paid appeal review hours
Check qualified posted local work after 2036 loss if net pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my claims wage could disappear before I have the safety credential for vehicle inspection. Written cut notice, paid training with protected hours and a real qualified offer covering our mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what a repair estimate leaves out. A driver needs to know a real person checked the photograph before refusing a damaged part.

headlineQuote: A driver needs to know a real person checked the photograph before refusing a damaged part.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old motor-claims lead** with a bachelor’s degree and above-typical pay.
He and Bea **pay a mortgage**, have no children and hold eight months of expenses.
He uses **AI occasionally** for email summaries and checks workshop bills against photographs.
He tests **paid inspection training** only with safety requirements, protected hours and a real opening.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his claims wage before he has vehicle-inspection credentials.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, protected paid training and a qualified offer covering their mortgage would help.
